utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please, Mr. Registrar. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First I would like to say good morning to the interpreters to be sure that everybody is ready. Good morning to the Prosecution and to the Defence and to the accused, and perhaps now we could have the witness, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, brought in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, here he is. Is everything working right? Did you rest up last night, Mr. Whatley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did all right, thank you, Mr. President. I did all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right, we can continue. Mr. Harmon, you have until a quarter after 12 and we will see how that works in with the breaks. Things are being timed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good morning Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning Counsel, and good morning Mr. Dundas-Whatley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you've heard, time is somewhat restricted in here, so my inquiry is going to be fairly focused, and even though I am going to be going through a large number of topics with you, still pause after I ask you a question so we don't make life more difficult for the translation section. Let me turn first, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, to your testimony about the 7th Muslim Brigade. The essence of your testimony was that the 7th Muslim Brigade had a destabilising effect in areas where there were Croats living; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, the 7th Muslim Brigade arrived in Travnik in March of 1993, if I recall your testimony correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly when they arrived in Travnik, it was about then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are other factors as well as the 7th Muslim Brigade that destabilised the situation in Central Bosnia; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the seizure by the HVO of power, of complete power in the municipality of Vitez, Kiseljak and Busovaca have a destabilising effect on the situation in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't aware that the HVO had taken power in Vitez municipality, had prevented the Muslims from working in the government and in the police departments, unless they swore an oath of allegiance to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, rather stupidly, I thought you meant electric power. I'm very sorry. Yes, I think the Croats civilian structures, political structures, the way they behaved was probably quite, could be described as antagonistic, and it did have, I think, yes, a destabilising effect, generally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did the fact that Herceg-Bosna had created a state within a legitimate state of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, also tend to destabilise the situation in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that had the Croats not separated from the Muslims, then by definition the situation would have been stable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the take-over of political and military power in the Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak municipalities occurred before the arrival of the 7th Muslim Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- to the extent that -- I think, if I could clarify. I know what you're saying, and I think you're basically right; but the municipalities that we're referring to, you've listed three, but of course we were dealing with about six, some of them were very much under the control of one side, some were very much of under the control of the other side, and some were divided politically or shared power politically. In the case of Vitez it was divided, the shared power never existed, certainly after January of 1993. So, there were two separate governments operating in the same area, two separate local governments. But in other areas, for example, Travnik, the Muslims were very much in control, they were the government in Travnik. Then in Kiseljak, the Croats were the government. It was more down to who had the, which population group had control of the town, and that was normally down to who was the largest population there at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the 7th Muslim Brigade take a headquarters in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember if they ever put a flag up in the town. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We have a slight problem here. If you don't mind, would you answer, please turn to the Judges and look at them. I know it's not really easy, but your answers should be directed at the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, you testified yesterday briefly about flag raising, both in the context of the 7th Muslim Brigade in Travnik raising its flag with a crescent and a star and the flag raising of Croat flags after the visit of Mate Boban on the 8th of April, 1993. Those kinds of displays tended also to destabilised the situation at various specific locations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Flags and other nationalist symbols take on a meaning, a gravity far beyond what we would expect here in western Europe. So the raising of somebody else's flag or the wearing of somebody else's badge had a very inflammatory effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me focus just briefly, if I can, for a moment, on the Travnik and Novi Travnik area. You testified on direct examination about tensions that existed in the Travnik and the Novi Travnik areas after the 10th of April, 1993; but there were tensions that existed in the Travnik and Novi Travnik area between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims before the 10th of April, 1993; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the incidents that you recounted to the Court only provide to the Court a very partial picture of the tensions that existed over a fairly long period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from the day we arrived in October, '92, Novi Travnik and Vitez and Busovaca, by the end of October, 1992, all three of those towns had seen Muslim Croat fighting on the streets and Muslim Croat deaths on the streets prior the end of October, 1992 when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could show the witness Defence Exhibit 419.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 419, while it's on its way to you, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, is a one-page annexe to a MILINFOSUM that you were shown yesterday, and it is the conclusions of a joint commission, and you are mentioned in that particular Defence Exhibit 419 as going to be a participant in the joint commission. Do you recognise that particular document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document that is the conclusions of a joint commission, and it has the names of Filip Filipovic and Mehmed Alagic underneath it. Did you participate in this joint commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this joint commission tend to reduce tensions, in your opinion, in the Travnik area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 16th of April, 1993, when fighting broke out in Vitez and Busovaca, was there any fighting between the HVO and the ABiH, or any significant fighting between the HVO and the army in the Travnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not fighting that could be -- not that was commanded from a high level. There was street fighting to some extent between the various factions, but at a much lower level, a local level, on the streets of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did it appear to you, then, that the commission had some ameliorative effect on the situation, on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What does ameliorative mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It remedied, it mitigated the situation, in terms of the violence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the two commanders in Travnik were very concerned to ensure that what was happening elsewhere did not happen in their town; and so, yes, the commission was successful for a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to Novi Travnik. In that particular municipality, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, you testified that on the 13th of April the HVO commander, Zeljko Sabljic informed you that three of his officers had been kidnapped, do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there after, a joint commission was set up to investigate the disappearance of those kidnapped officers, and when I say a joint commission, I'm talking about a commission between the ABiH, the Armija, and the HVO; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe there was also a member of the ECMM in that commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Now, on the 16th of April, when fighting broke out in Vitez and Busovaca, was there fighting between the HVO and the Armija in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, I can't remember. If I could just refer to my notebook, and maybe a MILINFOSUM or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. Dubuisson, if you could get Defence Exhibit 303.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, once again, I want to say when a document is put on the ELMO, at least for a little while, the monitors in the gallery should also have access to it, because this is a public hearing, they may be people from universities here and there may be people from other places that would be interested in following the hearing as comfortably as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Of course, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My notebook is not very illuminating about the situation in Novi Travnik on the 16th. However, I did have, I did have a meeting in Novi Travnik on the morning of the 16th. And at the meeting it was a joint meeting with the Bosnian army and the HVO, and there was, appears to be a certain amount of tension, but I don't think there was any shooting at all, certainly nothing in my notebook. It was more concerned with prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, let me show you Defence Exhibit 303, you have 303A in front of you, which is the English version, and this is a Defence Exhibit that was presented and it is a report from the brigade Commander, Zeljko Sabljic. It is dated the 18th of April 1993 at 0100 hours. It is sent to the Central Bosnia Operative Zone commander in Vitez. Let me just direct your attention to the introductory paragraph that refers to the further work of the HVO and the Armija Joint Commission in investigating the case of the kidnapping of the officers from the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade on the 13th of April. This is a report, as you can see, and if you would take a look at paragraphs 1 and 3, for just a moment, I'm going to ask awe couple of questions about it. Have you had a chance to read paragraphs 1 and 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It appears that this report indicates that the HVO and the Bosnian army continued its joint work after the attack that took place in Ahmici, after the attack that took place in Vitez and Busovaca on the 16th of April; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They continued to co-operate and work together in attempt to solve a crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think this is indicative of the general mood at the time between the HVO and the Bosnian army. The general mood was that they did not want to continue to prosecute this war, they did not want acts of kidnappings, massacres, burning of villages and joint command, joint commissions were being established all over the place in an attempt to stop what was happening and there was very good co-operation at low levels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in your opinion, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, was the ABiH receptive to the idea of investigating crimes that were committed presumably by one side or the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think both -- I believe -- it's a long time ago, but I believe both sides were keen to ensure that these things didn't continue, and to investigate the crimes they knew about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me just take you one step further in this, and ask you, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, whether the HVO representatives with whom you met or any HVO representatives ever approached you or any other third party, or the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in an effort to set up a joint commission for the investigation of the crimes at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was never approached. I personally was never approached with a view to establishing a joint commission to investigate Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of any effort by the HVO to engage the Armija in a joint investigation of either the crimes at Ahmici, the truck bomb at Stari Vitez, or the shelling of Zenica that occurred on the 19th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the case of Ahmici, I know that Bob Stewart spoke to Colonel Blaskic about this, which was many days after the event when we eventually realised the gravity and the scale of the crime. I believe, and I wasn't privy to that meeting, but I believe the result of it was quite positive in that I believe Colonel Blaskic, I believe he wanted to investigate it, as well, and asked for the help of UNPROFOR and of the British in that investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ask for the help of the Bosnian army or the Bosnian Muslim authorities in the investigation? In that investigation or the investigation of the truck bomb or the investigation of the shelling of Zenica on the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if he specifically asked for that, but I know that the HVO and the Bosnian army put a lot of effort and a lot of support into the joint commission that existed consisting of Franjo Nakic from the HVO and Dzemal Merdan from the Bosnian army 3 corps and I know this commission was very much supported by Colonel Blaskic and by General Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question is more specific, Mr. Dundas-Whatley. Did the HVO ever ask, to your knowledge, the Bosnian Muslim authorities, to participate in a joint investigation with them, the HVO, of the crimes that took place at Ahmici, at Stari Vitez, the truck bomb, and the shelling of Zenica on the 19th of April, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that question is better directed to Colonel Bob Stewart, who would know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me turn your attention to the 15th and 16th of April, 1993, in Travnik and in Vitez. Your testimony yesterday was that you were in Travnik attending a parade of the first anniversary celebration of the founding of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina when you were informed that Zivko Totic had been kidnapped and you received that information on the 15th of April 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I was informed exactly what had happened that was so important that I went to Zenica. I think I was informed of that later. Probably, I think I was informed of that later, probably over the radio, as I was either travelling to Zenica or once I had arrived there. I don't think I was informed of that while I was in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before Zivko Totic was kidnapped were you aware Colonel Blaskic had given a preparatory combat order at 10.00 in the morning on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no knowledge or access to combat orders, as I stated yesterday, of either side, we were not privy to their plans for fighting the war. That was of no concern of ours, and it was of -- and they certainly were not going to tell us what they were going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. I just want to note counsel has misstated the evidence. Totic was kidnapped at 8.30 a.m., an hour and a half before the referenced order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine, if that's the case, Mr. President, the facts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, when one of the parties recalls a witness's own words, I think that first and foremost the witness should say whether he agrees or doesn't. Thank you for your diligence and for your assistance, but I think that is the responsibility of the witness to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: With due respect, Mr. President, the question was, were you aware that Blaskic issued an order at 10.00 before Totic was kidnapped? The evidence in this case is that Totic was kidnapped at 8.30. He consults that the time was 10.00, that's what I was trying to note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, if you come in each time in place of your witness, we're never going to finish here. Let me turn to Mr. Dundas-Whatley, he is the one who has to answer, I'm sorry to say. After all, you will have a moment, you will have a time when you can ask further questions. Continue, please, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen such an order, preparatory combat order issued by General Blaskic on the 15th of April at 10.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen any combat orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I please have Defence Exhibit 267 and 268, please, and ask that those be shown to Mr. Dundas-Whatley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you another question, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, while those exhibits are being obtained, were you aware that on the 15th of April 1993 that Colonel Blaskic issued an order to take action at 1545 hours to all his brigade commanders? In other words, an order to increase their combat readiness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just have to repeat my answer from before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you one additional question and I expect to get the same answer, but have you seen that order, the order that he issued on the 15th of April at 1545 hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Have I seen it since then?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen some documents in preparation for this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was 10.45, not 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There's two, Judge Riad. There is one at 1000 hours on April 15th and there's one at 1545 hours on April 15th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen those orders even in preparation for this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During preparation for this case I have seen various documents, some of which were produced by the HVO. I can't remember specifically, if I see it, I may recognise it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, these documents are being prepared now by the registrar and they will be shown to you in just a moment?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you will allow, let me draw your attention to the fact that 268 has a bis version, which is confidential. I assume that the parties are in agreement that we can use the public version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's start, if we can, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, with 267, and you should have the English version in front of you. Have you seen that document before today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may have, it is similar to some I have seen. I may have seen it. There are things about it that I recognise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me just very quickly -- we're going to use this document throughout the morning, but let me just draw your attention to this. This is an order from General Blaskic, then Colonel Blaskic, dated April 15th. It is timed at 1000 hours and it is an order for preparatory combat command and it's been issued to all the commanders of his brigades, 1 through 12, and the commanders of the independent units, including the independent unit the Vitezovi. Now, let me show you 268, if you would look at 268, as well. 268 is the order that was issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 15th of April at 1545 hours and it is an order to take action and it has been issued to all his brigade commanders. Is that a document, sir, that you have seen prior to today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one is less familiar. I don't think I've ever seen this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if you just put those aside for a minute, I would like to carry on with the examination in respect of the evening of the 15th of April in Vitez when you visited the town commander Sefkija Dzidic and you testified that you met with him on, from what I gather, three occasions 1955 hours, 2100 hours and 2130 hours. At one of those meetings he informed you that three ABiH military policemen had been arrested at 1715 hours and that the arrestees had been taken to the elementary school at Dubravica. Do you remember your testimony about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are aware of the fact that's been established in this case that the Dubravica school is the headquarters of the Dubravica Knights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew the Dubravica school was a HVO location and it was quite often a check point outside it as well. But I was not sure -- it was no concern to me which unit was based there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on in one of your meetings with town commander Djidic, he said that -- he made a further complaint to you. He said that some ABiH soldiers had been disarmed and arrested; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those people had been disarmed and arrested by Stara Bila. Now, if you could take a look at Defence Exhibit 257, which is the order issued on the 15th of April 1993 at 10.00. Let me direct your attention, if I can, to paragraph 2.2 which is on the second page. Now, let me read that. Paragraph 2.2 reads as follows -- I see there is an error in the transcript. The transcript says "Defence Exhibit 257," it should be Defence Exhibit 267. So if that could be corrected. Now, Mr. Dundas-Whatley let me read 2.2. "The special purpose battalion Vitezovi will act on special assignment in the event of a break through in the Defence lines. Its assignment is to prevent enemy action in particular from the direction of Stari Vitez where the ABiH MP, which means Military Police, the Civilian Muslim Police and the PDV ABiH, are located with the probable assignment to act against the high command of the Operative Zone." I will not read the rest of that paragraph. Does it now seem to you Mr. Dundas-Whatley that the arrest of the ABiH military policemen and their being taken to the Dubravica school was the result of the order issued to the Vitezovi by Colonel Blaskic at 10.00 in the morning on the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're asking me to answer a question about a document that's here in front of me, and so I'm studying this document now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. I direct your attention primarily to the sentence in paragraph 2.2 that references the Military Police and Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I look at this document across the whole, and I haven't read every word of it, this document gives me the impression that the HVO headquarters in Vitez was scared stiff, was very, very worried that Colonel Blaskic was worried that he was about to be attacked. That is the impression the document gives me, rightly or wrongly, but that's what he says in paragraph 1. He then goes into paragraph 2.2, and he's apparently giving an order to a unit and telling them to prevent enemy action for a particular location, because there are various units in that location which he believes are about to attack his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Including the Military Police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he draws attention to the Military Police and suggests that they are likely to attack his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question to you is, does it seem likely in light of this particular order, given to the Vitezovi at 10.00 in the morning on the 15th of April, 1993 that the reason those military policemen were arrested by the Vitezovi and taken to their headquarters is a result of this order issued by General Blaskic at 10.00 in the morning on the 15th? Is that a fair conclusion to draw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is nothing in here that is issuing orders to address anyone, to killing anyone, to attack anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not defending the action of the unit concerned, but I'm referring directly to this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that the arrest of the Armija soldiers at Stari Bila -- again, the name Darko Kraljevic surfaced in that particular incident, and Darko Kraljevic was the commander of the Vitezovi. Do you think that in any way relates to this particular order of General Blaskic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, this is the third time that you're asking the question. You're deducing from an order that was issued at 10.00, and you were asking that the witness answer the question three times. I think it's time to move to another question. You have a hypothesis you want to have the witness verify, but nonetheless, I think you must move to another question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. President, let me -- if you keep those documents near you, we're going to use those documents again, Mr. Dundas-Whatley. Let me turn to a different area, and that is certain conversations that Colonel Blaskic had in respect of who was responsible for Ahmici. Were you present when Colonel Blaskic had a conversation with Brigadier Alistair Duncan about who was responsible for the commission of the crimes at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because Colonel Duncan, as he was then, arrived one day, I think, one or two days, I think, before we left. I don't remember that meeting. I may have been there but I very much doubt it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me summarise what Brigadier Duncan related to this court about that conversation. He was asked a question, and -- about Ahmici, and the explanation of that, and according to the testimony of Brigadier Duncan this is what he answered: "From Blaskic was either it had been done by Muslim extremists who had somehow come into the Vitez pocket and committed this event and disappeared in the night on their own people, or indeed Muslim armed forces from the BiH, or finally the Muslims dressed up in HVO uniform." Those were the three reasons given. I'm sorry, I should refresh that. The three reasons were, and these are the people he informed -- these are the people Blaskic informed Duncan were responsible for the commission of the crimes at Ahmici. The three reasons given were Serb extremists, Muslims who had infiltrated the pocket or Muslims dressed in HVO uniforms. Now, what is your reaction, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, to the proposition that the Serbs were responsible for the commission of the crimes at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think that's a truthful answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be almost impossible, Your Honours, for the Serbs, who were 20 kilometres away to come to Ahmici to commit that atrocity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think that that answer to Brigadier Duncan was a truthful answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That Colonel Blaskic was telling the truth. ?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no -- I don't know what made Colonel Blaskic think that the Serbs could possibly have done that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, in respect of whether the proposition that Muslims had come into the village of Ahmici, torched the village, killed over a hundred people, driven all the Muslims out of the village of Ahmici, what's your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's slightly a bizarre thing to say and I think it's so unlikely that the Muslims could possibly have done that to themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We go to the third component of this answer, and that is that the Muslims disguised themselves as HVO and went in and did that. What was your reaction to that, Mr. Dundas-Whatley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's ridiculous to even suggest that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me talk to you again about another statement in respect of the investigation into Ahmici that was given by Colonel Blaskic, this time in an Article that appeared in October of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Beyond the scope, Mr. President. I've let it go on but this is beyond the scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's out of the scope, yes, if you look at things strictly, but the witness had the functions of liaison officer. I don't think there's any problem with asking him questions about the very core of his mission. He was a liaison officer, he represents the liaison between various military, political and other powers. Therefore, there's nothing wrong with the Prosecution asking what he might think about opinions that the accused may have offered as explanations for the massacre at Ahmici. Continue, please, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley I'm going to read from Prosecutor's Exhibit 380. There's no reason to put it in front of you. I'll read a portion verbatim. This is an interview of Colonel Blaskic that appeared in the magazine (phoen) Danis in October of 1993. Mr. Blaskic -- Colonel Blaskic was asked the following question: "You investigated a crime in Ahmici. What is the result of the investigation so far?" And Colonel Blaskic answered as follows: "The investigation is still in progress. Information is being gathered. In any case, this is a well-planned scenario in which Muslim forces wanted, once again, to cast a blemish on units of the HVO before the world community. After the crimes that Muslim forces committed in the areas around the Croatian villages of Lasva, Dusina, Gusti Grab and other villages in the Busovaca municipality, the case of Ahmici was staged and skilfully shown to foreign reporters and the EC observer mission with the assistance of the commander of the British battalion at the time, Bob Stewart. So far we are certain that the crime was committed by members of the HOS (Croatian defence force) in Zenica, which was mostly Muslim, and parts of the Muslim forces of the MOS (Muslim defence force) and I have already said that this investigation is continuing. It is certain that the HVO does not stand behind the crime that others desire to attribute to us. However, I want to say that a much greater crime is being skilfully concealed. Muslim forces shot to death more than 40 civilians, mostly women and children, back at the beginning of June in the village of Mojina (phoen), Travnik municipality. We have not been allowed to this day, nor has the UNHCR, or the International Red Cross or the European Observer Mission to look around that area and perform an exhumation of the bodies. That was a collective execution in front of other Croats who had to dig the grave for those who were killed." Now, let me ask you your reaction to portions of this statement attributed to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, would it be possible for me to have a copy just to make notes on it, because there was a lot contained in that. I'm afraid I've cleverly forgotten to bring a pen. If the usher could lend me a pen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me take advantage of this break in order to say that in the French version of the official document from the registry as regards possibly point -- point of view, is that the English version -- could you go back to the middle of the paragraph and see -- "I've already declared that the investigation was ongoing." Do you see that? "I already have declared," it says in French --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And in the next sentence, at least in the French version, is a bit different. Mine says, that is from -- the document from the registry, it is certain, these are the words attributed to General Blaskic in the interview, "It's certain that the HVO is not responsible for the crime that some people would like to ascribe to us." In what you read, which was interpreted, I didn't get the same version. It was more ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you repeat it, please, and the interpreters can try to help me. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "It is certain that the HVO does not stand behind the crime that others desire to attribute to us."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. It's not the same. Let me call your attention to the fact that the version I have here is different. Here it is certain -- the accused says, according to this, "It is certain that the HVO is not responsible for the crimes that certain parties wish to ascribe to it." I would ask that at the proper time this be checked and compared with the Serbo-Croatian version because you have that one in front of you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, your reaction, first of all, to the second sentence in the article, "In any case, this is a well-planned scenario which Muslim forces wanted, once again, to cast a blemish on the units of the HVO before the world community." What's your reaction to that? Do you think the massacre at Ahmici was a well-planned scenario, that the Muslim forces wanted to use and did perpetrate in order to cast a blemish on the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think that's what he's saying. Could I just have a minute to read this, please, this whole thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you read the document, Mr. Dundas-Whatley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm still reading. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: After the review of the document, I suggest that we take a 15 minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've read the document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Since -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, what is your reaction to this -- these comments of Colonel Blaskic in respect of the -- it being a well-planned scenario in which Muslim forces wanted, once again, to cast a blemish on the forces of the HVO before the world community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are two things that spring to mind about this, and, firstly, I think that Colonel Blaskic is using this military publication for normal -- for military propaganda reasons as every army uses its own military publications. But secondly, I get the impression from reading this that probably Colonel Blaskic actually didn't know who committed the events in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? In what regard?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me read this. "So far we are certain," and I underscore the word "certain" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's not waste time, Mr. Dundas-Whatley. Yes, on this point all of the versions are the same. It says that we're certain that the crime was committed on that day. On that particular point all of the versions are in agreement with one another.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not disputing that, Mr. President. It's in relation to who he thinks has done it. He's -- on one hand he's blaming people, the HOS from Zenica and saying they're mostly Muslims, which I have already said I think is ridiculous and I don't think he would have believed at the time, and then he's blaming the MOS, the Muslim defence force, and then he says the investigation is continuing. I think he's trying to put on a brave face about something which he doesn't appear to know much about, because if he had conducted a proper investigation in this stage in October or whenever this is, he would, I think by now he would have stated exactly who was commanding the attack against Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions in respect to this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I suggest that we take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing, have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, you were asked yesterday a number of questions about command and control by Defence counsel, and the first question you were asked was essentially a question about the degree of command and control in the HVO and Central Bosnia while you were there. I'm going to try to distil your answer: Essentially you answered that it was difficult for you to make that kind of an assessment of the degree of command and control that Blaskic had over the forces in Central Bosnia. You didn't have detailed information about the workings of the HVO headquarters in Vitez, and you did not have access to combat orders; and, therefore, you opined that the degree of command and control in Central Bosnia was poor. Does that fairly characterise your testimony in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does not. My opinion that command and control was poor was based on a variety --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment, please. There is a technical problem here in the public gallery. What's wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the time being, for technical reasons, we can't have retransmission into the gallery, so the video is going to be interrupted for a few moments, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, we will suspend as long as it takes so that the gallery can follow the hearing as well. The hearing is suspended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, as we do in matches, we're going to count this technical time, which was needed to make the repairs. I suppose we will take our break at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, yesterday when you were asked questions about the degree of command and control in Central Bosnia, you said it was difficult for you to make that kind of assessment because you did not have detailed information about the workings of the HVO headquarters in Vitez, you did not have access to combat orders, some of the indicators to you that command and control was poor, was based on the poor quality of officers and soldiers in the HVO, the poor communications of the HVO, the divided loyalties between village and between central staff, and you used examples to illustrate your point, illustrations of an example at a checkpoint and cease-fire violations. As a result of that, you opined that command and control was poor in Central Bosnia. Let me ask you this question: No system of command and control functions perfectly in any army, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the British system is pretty good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is insubordination in the British army, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not the level we are discussing here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, but there is insubordination in the British army. On occasions some officers refuse to follow orders; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Over small issues over small periods of time, there are occasionally differences of opinion which could be characterised as you have said, but not -- to describe the British army as having a poor command and control is very misleading.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the level of insubordination in the former JNA; do you have any idea about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's difficult to compare, isn't it, the British army, which is one of the best armies in the world, to other armies in the world; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I served in the British army, I know a lot about it, and I know certain about the Bosnian army and the HVO, and that was the extent of my comparison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me ask you, you were read a quote yesterday, as well, and the quote you were read was as follows: "The attack on Ahmici could not have occurred without the authority of Colonel Blaskic due to the number of troops involved and the scale of the attack." Your answer to the answer of whether you agreed or disagreed with that was that you disagreed and you stated as follows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, there is an objection from Mr. Hayman. Does the objection have to do with what the witness said?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The question was authority and order of Colonel Blaskic, the transcript will so reflect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The answer that you stated was, quote, "I disagree. The statement assumes that all the attacks would have been ordered by Blaskic, and the command and control that existed at the time means it is probably not the case, almost certainly not the case." Now, let me draw your attention, first of all, to the issue of cease-fires. In the period of time in and around, from April 16th to April - to the end of April, there were a number of cease-fires, were there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of cease-fires, and in the months before that, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm focusing -- please just answer my questions, Mr. Dundas-Whatley. In the month of April, between the 16th and the end of the month, there were a number of cease-fires; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sometimes cease-fires were not followed because, if you will, there was hot blood between the combatants and they didn't want to put down their arms; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get the sense, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, that on other occasions a cease-fire order would be issued for public consumption, but privately and behind the scenes there was another agenda, that is, an agenda to pursue the combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is possible, but I did not get that impression. But I'm not saying it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there are other instances, are there not, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, where the cease-fires were coming in a relatively quick succession, that it was difficult to impose immediate and absolute cease-fire before there was a breach.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were successive cease-fires, some were within two or three days of each other; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And more frequently occasionally, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And more frequently. Okay. Now, let me ask you, you said that one of your indicators as to why there was poor command and control in Central Bosnia was because of poor quality of officers and the poor quality of soldiers. Did you ever do an analysis or a survey on the level of training and the military background of Blaskic's subordinate commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to a general impressions that I gained from talking to these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Did you do an analysis or a survey of the training and military background of Blaskic's subordinate commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk briefly about the JNA. The JNA, was it not, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, one of the largest armies in eastern Europe, before the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a very large conscript army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was a very formidable, potentially a formidable foe even for the British army; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what we believed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you said there was conscription, there was universal conscription for all young men of the age, I think, of 18, and they had to serve a year in the JNA, and they had to receive training in the JNA; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the former Yugoslavia there were professional military academies, including the Military Academy in Belgrade where then Colonel Blaskic graduated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know a little bit about his former military experience because somebody told me at the time, and it is true, yes, he did study at the Military Academy at Belgrade, and I believe he reached the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the reserve officer training program that existed in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know very little about it, but what I do know is that people were, the reserve officers were promoted over a period of time, and the age you may leave the JNA as a lieutenant or captain, and a few years later be a major, and a few years later a lieutenant colonel, but with no command responsibility and no military training during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you start your military career in the reserves of the British army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, the concept of territoriality, local defence, the JNA had a principle, did they not, of the Territorial Defence, and those forces were based in villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what existed before the collapse of Yugoslavia. I know there was a Territorial Defence system in, loosely in place when I arrived in October, '92. What happened before then I do not know anything about at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that one of the central pillars of the JNA, the total national defence philosophy was to have Territorial Defence units in local villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Now, did you ever attend any of the training or were you familiarised with any of the training that was available to conscripts in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, you're unable to give us, are you, in your own words, the standards and the degree of training that was available to JNA conscripts in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I know very little about it, about how the training was conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, one of the fundamental concepts of the former JNA and one of the fundamental concepts of the HVO was the concept of unity of command, which is the concept of subordination; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, when you say, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, that the level of, the poor quality of soldier that existed in Central Bosnia, are you ignoring the fact that a significant number of those people who were soldiers in the HVO had undergone mandatory military training in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I'm not ignoring anything. I'm reiterating my opinion at the time, based on the information told to me by the Bosnian army commanders and the HVO commanders about the problems they had with their soldiers, in particular, most of the soldiers came from villages and never attended the training in the JNA before the war, most of them were illiterate, most of them didn't-- a lot of them didn't know what they were supposed to be doing, they were not formed into proper units. I must say it was particularly true on the side of the Bosnian army because there were huge numbers of refugees they had to deal with in Travnik. My testimony is not based on anything to do with the JNA. It's based on what I found talking, as the person whose responsibility it was to talk to military commanders in Bosnia about such matters. It was they that were forwarding this information to me about the huge problems they had with their command and control, huge problems they had with their soldiers. It was them that was telling me, and I'm just reiterating that to this Court as honestly and as directly as I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, if the HVO and the ABiH commanders had such poor quality soldiers and officers, how did they stop and defend against the Republika Srpska juggernaut that was better armed, that inherited all the equipment that was available from the former JNA? How did they do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the front-lines stopped moving when the Serbs had taken 70 per cent of the country; and so, I think that to say that 65 per cent of the population were now living in 30 per cent of the country, and you attribute that with some military achievement; it was a massive disaster.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was: How did the HVO, with an army, as you put it, of illiterate peasants and the ABiH with an army of illiterate peasants, successfully defend the lines against the VRS? How did they do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not go to the front-lines very much. How they fought on the front-lines, I'm not aware of. I'm just trying to tell you exactly what I -- exactly as I can what I knew and what I was told. To suggest that the HVO and the Bosnian army jointly conducted some wonderful defence of Bosnia is meaningless, they lost thousands of men on those front-lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me change the topic slightly. Mr. Dundas-Whatley, have you seen any other combat orders issued by Colonel Blaskic before you testified here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may have, I have reviewed quite a number of documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have Prosecutor's Exhibit 267 and 268 in front of you? Those are the two exhibits we looked at a little earlier today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, first of all, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, to Prosecutor's Exhibit 268 -- I'm sorry, 267, and this is a preparatory order issued at 10.00 on the 15th of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For the record, Counsel, these a Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me refer you, please, to paragraph 2.1 of that order, and I would like to refer you to the following sentence which is found at the bottom of the first full paragraph, and it reads as follows: "In the event of a rather strong attack by the Muslim extremist forces from the directions of the villages of Nadioci, Ahmici, Sivrino, Pirici, inform me," which is Colonel Blaskic who is the author of this order, "and if fire is opened directly at you, return the fire and neutralise the attacker." Now, let me turn your attention to the next exhibit, Defence Exhibit 268, and this is a combat, I mean, an order to take action that is dated the 15th of April at 1545 hours, it is addressed to all the brigade commanders listed in the right-hand column as addressees, and let me direct your attention to paragraph 2.2, which essentially orders that all of the units, the brigades and the military, 4th Military Police Battalion increase their combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 2. what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 2.1. Let me then turn you to the end of the document, if I can, paragraph 6, where Colonel Blaskic orders that "Regular reports are to be sent in by 1800 hours in the evening and 0600 hours in the morning, special reports as need may be." Now, this reporting back feature, this request to get, receive reports back from your subordinate units is a normal factor found in armies, isn't it? You want to know what your troops are doing, you want them to report back to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but in the British army we don't give subordinates orders to report, because it is in their training and they know they have to report anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Defence Exhibit 269, please, shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, this is a combat command issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 16th of April at 0130 hours. It is issued to the commander of the HVO Brigade Vitez, Mr. M. Cerkez and PN units Tvrtko; have you seen this document before you testified today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to paragraph 2, this particular paragraph orders Mr. Cerkez to assign his forces to occupy the defence region blockade villages and prevent all entrances to and exits from the villages. "In the event of open attack by the Muslims, neutralise them and prevent their movement with precise fire from PN." And the time for readiness of this particular order is 5.30 in the morning on the 16th of April, 1993. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, Colonel Blaskic advises commander Cerkez of the positions of various elements of his forces; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you aware, sir, that -- well, let me rephrase the question. The evidence in this case shows that the HVO engaged in simultaneous attacks on the villages of Ahmici, Vitez, Nadioci, Santici, Pirici, Sivrino Selo and Donji Vecerska on the morning of 16 April at 5.30 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you asking me am I aware?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew it was about that time, I thought it was a little later actually, but about that time of the morning war did break out in many locations, probably the ones you just said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could I have Defence Exhibits 283, 282 and 281 shown to the witness? Now, let's start, Mr. Dundas-Whatley --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Am I going to have to refer back to these?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to keep those up there, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, if we could start with Defence Exhibit 282, if the -- the Exhibits I'm going to show you now are other combat related orders. This order which, is Defence Exhibit 282, is order an issued by Colonel Blaskic on the morning of the 6th -- I'm sorry, 16th April, 1993 at 1940 hours, and it is issued to the commander of the 4th Military Police battalion in Vitez and to the commander of the Travnika Brigade for information, and it relates to the withdrawal of troops of the Travnik Military Police company to Vitez. If you -- it's a command, and it is a command, and you will see in paragraph one it relates to the unit of the 4th Military Police battalion that's currently in Travnik, and it is a command to transfer them to Vitez. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you see in paragraph 2 that the transfer should be carried out in small groups depending on the conditions that existed, and bearing in mind security. Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the purpose of this order was to reinforce the Viteska Brigade. Do you see that in the introductory paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, do I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Viteska Brigade was engaged in combat in the Vitez municipality on the 16th of April. You're aware of that; aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know which brigades were fighting, but it's pretty obvious that every member of the HVO would have been fighting by then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to Defence Exhibit 281. 281 is a one-page document in English, and this -- do you see that in front of you? It is a combat order dated the 16th of April, 1993 at 1945 hours. It is issued by Colonel Blaskic, and it is issued to the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinski Brigade in Busovaca and to Mr. Dusko Grubesic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I have, but I -- I don't think I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen the previous document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The subjects of it is vaguely familiar, so I may have read it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's return back to 281, the one document that is the combat order to Dusko Grubesic for the Defence of Kuber. And this particular document is a short document. As you can see, in paragraph 2 Colonel Blaskic identifies the task that he wants Dusko Grubesic and his brigade to undertake. That is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn your attention to Defence Exhibit 283 and ask you to examine 283. 283 is an order for increased control of the territory to the commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade in Novi Travnik, and it's dated 16 April, 1993 at 2015 hours and it is signed by Colonel Blaskic. Do you see -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just need to read it, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And paragraph 4 of that particular document, do you see that Colonel Blaskic asks that a report on the execution of the order be received by him by 2400 hours on 16 April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, he makes a similar type of request. I hate to refer you back, but would you look at 281 as well, which is the combat order to Dusko Grubesic to defend the positions on Kuber? You see in paragraph 4 that Colonel Blaskic says, "Report back to me in writing"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you some other combat orders, if I could. Could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/45 and 456/46?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could I have the number again, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dundas-Whatley these are documents that -- at least 456/45 is a document I showed you yesterday. Do you remember this document? This is a document that is directed by Colonel Blaskic to the Ban Jelisic Brigade in Kiseljak. It's dated the 17th of April, 1993 at 2345 hours. You saw this document yesterday when I showed it to you; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, briefly. Unfortunately, I don't even recognise it from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen this document prior to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recognise this document at all for some reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this is a document that in paragraph 2.2 -- it is an order for the combat operations, and in paragraph 2.2 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, to interrupt. This is bit -- this paragraph I recognise, which you drew my attention to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me redirect your attention to that paragraph. Paragraph 2.2, this order for combat operations directs the Ban Jelisic Brigade to use artillery and fire preparations in a particular attack and to capture Gomionica and Svinjarevo and it describes how that particular task is to be accomplished. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That paragraph 2.2, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you turn to the back -- the second page of that, it indicates in the document that combat operations are to begin on April 18th at 5.30 in the morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And paragraph 11 indicates that the commander of the Ban Jelisic Brigade -- or the Ban Jelisic Brigade command is to report to Colonel Blaskic upon completing the assigned tasks, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me -- take a glance at the whole document for just a minute, because I want to ask you if you've ever seen this document before. I showed it to you yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so. I only recognise the paragraph that you drew my attention to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Now, let me turn your attention next to another combat order, and this is a combat order which is the next Exhibit that you were handed. It should be 456/46. It's a combat order dated the 18th of April, 1993 at 1.40 -- 0140 hours, and it's directed to a different part of Colonel Blaskic's area of operations, that is to Foinijca, and it is an order that directs that the commander of the Fojnica HVO battalion engage in certain combat activities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before I presented it to you today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is familiar. I may well have been shown it by the Defence attorney, but I'm not entirely certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it you don't have a clear recollection of ever having seen this document, it's possible but you're not entirely sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I'm not entirely certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Turn to paragraph 6 of that particular exhibit. Again, you can see, can you not, the last sentence in that, Colonel Blaskic requests that a report be made to him regularly on all activities, as well as the implementation of the assignment. Isn't that correct? He's asking for a report back; isn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the evidence that has been presented in this case, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, is on the morning of the 18th of April, at 5.30 in the morning, the villages of Gomionica and Svinjarevo were attacked by the HVO. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that these villages were razed to the ground and all the Muslims were driven out of these villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm -- could you tell me the names of the villages again, and maybe if I look at the map I can refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Svinjarevo and Gomionica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The fighting in Gomionica, just for the record, went on for six weeks, contrary to counsel's statement, but I don't want to interrupt him otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I assist the witness? I can direct him more quickly, Mr. President. I can show him where the villages are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, approach the witness. For the time being he doesn't seem to be very aware of that. Mr. Nobilo, Mr. Hayman, if you would like to approach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He's indicated, Mr. President, for the record, and the witness can indicate that I've pointed out the villages of Svinjarevo and Gomionica to him. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really, because those villages were in the Kiseljak municipality, which was well beyond my scope of interest and responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me show you the -- some responses that were made by Blaskic's subordinate commanders. In fact, one of the indicia of command and control, I'm sure you will agree with me on this, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, is when a commander gives a request -- an order to a subordinate to report back, that the subordinate reports back. That's a favourable indication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, don't make too many comments, ask the question, because that's a long way of going about it. And let me remind you of your scheduling needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm very conscious of it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That a favourable indication that command and control are functioning properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One indication, yes, of good command and control is if you ask for a report from a subordinate that he gives you that report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I have, please, Prosecutor's Exhibit 521 and Defence Exhibit 280 shown to the witness. Now, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, I'm going to show you a sample of some of the responses made by Blaskic's subordinate commanders. I'm not going to show them all to you. And let me ask you -- we'll start -- We can start with 521, Mr. Usher. Do you have 521 in front you, Mr. Dundas-Whatley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a response -- an operative report on the situation at 6.00 in the morning on the 16th of April, 1993 from the Jure Francetic Brigade, Branislav Borzniak (phoen), and it indicates, does it not, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, and I will read it to you, "The night was quiet in the zone covered by the brigade. All units are holding the positions they had seized. The town is under control, and our units are letting unarmed civilians who are going to work to pass through." So this is an example, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, of the Zenica Brigade reporting back to Colonel Blaskic at 6.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm slightly confused about this, because I don't know which town he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in any event, whether -- I don't think that's particularly of interest which town, he's -- this is an indication that the Jure Francetic Brigade is reporting back to Colonel Blaskic at 6.00 in the morning on the situation at 6.00 in the morning on the 16th of April; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a report, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me show you Defence Exhibit 280. Do you have that in front of you? This is a report dated the 16th of April from Pasko Ljubicic, who was the Military Police, 4th Battalion commander. Do you have that report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you see the first paragraph, very short sentence that says, "Acting in accordance with your order number," and the number is given, "of 16 April, we hereby report." And you see that that is a report back by the 4th Military Police to Colonel Blaskic about the events that took place -- read the document for a moment if you care to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a report from -- yes. As you say, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know where the Bungalow is that is -- ever hear of that while you were a liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't ever remember the word "Bungalow".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the -- do you know where there was an A-frame shaped building located on the outskirts of the village of Ahmici? Did you ever see that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was that a restaurant that was subsequently burnt down?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know. It's an A-frame building. It may be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a building next to the road on a corner which the HVO -- which HVO soldiers used and were -- I think they were accommodated there. And following the attack on Ahmici some weeks later or maybe months later, I don't know, that building subsequently burnt down. And this building had been a restaurant, I think, or a large bar. Probably a restaurant. That could be the building you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me -- could I have the next exhibits, please, and that is the exhibits which would be 28 -- Defence 287, Defence 312 and Defence 325? By the way, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, this particular report, Defence 280, have you ever seen this report prior to testifying today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't recognise the report, but I may well have read it, but I did read quite a lot of documents over a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of reading this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall it, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, the next series of exhibits I'm going to show you, we can start with Defence Exhibit 287. 287. Mr. Dundas-Whatley, they are sample reports back to Colonel Blaskic from the Viteska Brigade, and you will notice that in the upper left-hand corner the source of these documents. The first document, Defence Exhibit 287, is a report dated the 17th of April at 6.00 in the morning, and it is a combat report, and the author of this report is Zvonimir Cilic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before coming in to testify today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is -- the content of this document is familiar, but I don't know if I've read it, or if it was read to me or something similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But this is a document, is it not, from the Viteska Brigade to Colonel Blaskic indicating the situation on the ground at 17 April at 6.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to the next -- another document, this is a day later, from the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which one is it, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is 312. And this is dated the 18th of April at 1600 hours. It is from the Viteska Brigade and it is to the Central Bosnia Operation Zone command, and it's an operations report. It is signed by the officer on duty, whose signature I can't read on the original, but let me ask you: In this operations report, there are a number of paragraphs and very briefly, let me just go over those paragraphs with you. In paragraph number one, it indicates that in the Kuber region the defenders were holding their particular positions. In paragraph number two, it indicates that in Gornji Santici, Mahala hamlet, there's heavy fighting. Further on reads, in the villages of Santici and Donja Dubravica there's fire. From the villages of Sivrino Selo and another village that I cannot pronounce. The third paragraph indicates the stretch of the defence lines, and it indicates they go from Krizancevo Selo, Krecivine and Jardol and remain unchanged. Further reports that in the area of paragraph 4, Divjak and Bila, there's constant firing. Paragraph 5 indicates that the Kruscica region continues to be under attack. So this is a fairly comprehensive report to Colonel Blaskic from the Viteska Brigade command on the 18th of April, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this a good quality summary -- a good quality report back to a commander about the events that are taking place in that particular region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the best one you've shown me so far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Have you ever seen this document before you testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
