utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you the last document from the Viteska Brigade, again a sample. This is a document, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, that is the following day. Now, this is the 19th of April, 1993, and this is addressed to the Central Bosnia operation zone command. It's an operations report. Again, the operations duty officer signed it, and this indicates, in the first paragraph, what the Muslim forces -- what regions they had shelled, it indicates further, in the second paragraph that pursuant to Colonel Blaskic's order of 19 April, the very same day this order was sent back, the report was sent back to Colonel Blaskic, that the road to Han Bila and Zepce had been blocked. In other words, Colonel Blaskic sent an order on the 19th of April 1993 and that order had been complied with. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And -- now, this is, again, an order from the Viteska Brigade informing Colonel Blaskic of the situation in that particular region; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before coming in to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me now turn to the next series of documents from Busovaca, and if I could have D277, D289, D292, D288, D313, D324 shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you still on the same subject, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps it would have been a bit easier if we could know if the Defence witness more or less agreed with the idea you're trying to express, that is, that there was a certain degree of good quality in the relationship and the chain of command, which would make things move forward more quickly; but of course, you are the one conducting the questioning, not myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for the suggestion, but given the fact the witness hasn't seen many of these documents, and I will go as quickly as I can with these documents, I think it is important that he at least inspect them. Could we start, Mr. Usher, with 277A, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, these are a series of documents coming from the Nikola Subic-Zrinski Brigade in Busovaca. And let me start out with 277A, an order, I'm sorry, a report to the Central Bosnia Operation Zone from that particular brigade in Busovaca, and it is a report on the situation of the brigade's zone of responsibility at 1700 hours. And it is signed -- let me direct your attention, first of all, to the first paragraph where there is a description of infantry attacks in particular identified regions, in the region of Gornji Rovna and Pezici, and further, there were combat activities in the region of Kuber and Obla Glava. Now, this is a report back to the commander from that particular brigade in Busovaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, then, to 289A. Again, this is a report back to the commander, and I say these are samples, this is a report back to the commander the following day, the 17th of April, 1993, at 8.30 in the morning, directed to Colonel Blaskic from the brigade commander, Dusko Grubesic; and it indicates that the brigade had lost its positions on Kuber and that Colonel Blaskic would be informed of any further activities. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me return to 292B -- 292, I'm sorry. This is a report, again, from the Busovaca Nikola Subic-Zrinski Brigade on 17 April, and it reports the situation in the zone of responsibility at 1200 hours. You can see that it is a report identifying regions that have been attacked and are engaged in combat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn you to the next exhibit, which is 288A, Defence Exhibit 288A. It is an exhibit dated the 17th of April, 1993 from the Nikola Subic-Zrinski Brigade to the Central Bosnia Operation Zone commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't been given that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have 288?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have 289, which we have been through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While Mr. Dubuisson is looking for 288, let me ask you a question with respect to the documents I've shown you thus far from the Busovaca Brigade. Have you seen any of these documents before you came in to testify, 289, 292 and 277?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably not, but there is a sort -- the general feeling that's coming from them is not unfamiliar, but I don't actually know which ones, if any of these, I've seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have any recollection of having seen these; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have 288A in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again, this is from the same brigade in Busovaca on the 17th of April, and this is an indication of where combat was taking place in that particular brigade's area of operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, on the 17th of April, these three documents which I have shown you, 289, Defence 289, Defence 292 and Defence 288 are multiple reports coming to Colonel Blaskic from the same brigade identifying and informing him of the combat activity that is taking place in the Busovaca region; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you Defence Exhibit 313, we can turn our attention to that, because this is now a report the following day. Do you have 313 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, just in case, the next exhibit after 313 would be 324.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, if you turn your attention to 313, this is dated, again, the 18th of April, the day after the three previous documents we have been talking about, and it is a report on the situation in the brigade's zone of responsibility at 1800 hours. In this document you can see that the operations officer on duty is reporting to Colonel Blaskic what the situation is in the area of operation for that particular brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention to 324, which is a sample of documents, Defence documents, if we could. You see that, now, this is a further report on the 19th of April. Now, this is the day after the previous report that you have seen, and it is coming from the Nikola Subic-Zrinski Brigade in Busovaca, and it is going to the Central Bosnia Operation Zone command to Colonel Blaskic, and it is signed by the brigade commander, Dusko Grubesic. Now, if you take a look at this document, this is a report in paragraph 1, you can see there are some asterisks in paragraph 1, and these identify not only the area where the attacks took place, but identify the enemy units that are being engaged. Do you see what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see in paragraph 2 the identification of the HVO forces, both, it identifies the first brigade with the first asterisk, the second brigade; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the standard way that I think these are going, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this a pretty good military report back to a commander, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly compared with the rest of them it's quite good, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before you came in to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, now, to the following exhibits, Defence Exhibit 305, 306, and Defence Exhibit 323. Now, you'll recall, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, that I showed you an earlier exhibit, and this was an exhibit that is Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/45. I referred you to the second paragraph that talked about, it was a combat order from Colonel Blaskic, and it indicated that the combat instructions were to capture Gomionica and Svinjarevo, and the combat operations were to start on the 18th of April at 5.30 in the morning. Do you remember what document I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have quite a large pile of these now. Could you give me the number, again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, 456/45, and it is an order for combat operations on the 17th of April, 1993 at 2345 hours to the Ban Jelacic Brigade command, and it is an order to commence combat operations the following morning at 5.30 on the villages of Gomionica and Svinjarevo. Turn to paragraph 2.2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turn to paragraph 2.2, just to refresh your recollection, and paragraph 10, which is the time the command is, the operation is supposed to start against those particular villages. Now we can turn our attention, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, to these three next exhibits, which represent samples of the Kiseljak Brigade's responding to Colonel Blaskic. Turn your attention first to Defence Exhibit 305. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a report from the officer on duty of the Ban Jelacic Brigade headquarters, a gentleman by the name of Mato Lucic, and this is a report on the situation in Kiseljak at 10.00 in the morning. If you turn your attention to paragraph 1b, it reads that, "Our forces which are fulfilling their tasks in the village of Gomionica are being attacked. They are mostly using snipers, a large number of forces has left Gomionica and pulled out toward the village of Stojkovici." And in the second paragraph it indicates that "Tasks are being done by orders." It goes on to state that the villages of Jelovac, Gromljak, Malva and Palez have been disarmed." So, this is a report from the Kiseljak commander, officer on duty, I should say, to Colonel Blaskic about the situation in respect of his order that he gave the night before about attacks Gomionica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to the next exhibit, which is the same day, 18 April, 1993, and this is a brief report from the brigade commander, Mijo Bozic, dated the 18th of April, 1993, at 1645 hours, in other words, later in the day, and it is a description of further conflicts in the area; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lastly, let me turn your attention to these Kiseljak documents, and turn your attention to 323. 323 is, again, from the Ban Jelacic Brigade, and it is a combat report for the 19th of April, 1993 at 2.00 in the morning, and it describes the Muslim armed forces in paragraph 1, and it describes the attempted counter-attack on Gomionica, and it describes a situation of the HVO forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in respect of these three documents I have shown you about Kiseljak, have you ever seen these three documents before you came in here to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it appears that there's reporting back to Colonel Blaskic about the military attack that he ordered on Svinjarevo and Gomionica; do they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, lastly, to Defence Exhibit 322. Mr. Dundas-Whatley, this is an exhibit, Defence Exhibit dated the 19th of April, 1993, and it is from the 111th XP Brigade located in Zepce, and one of the addressees is Colonel Blaskic. This is a report -- and by the way, Zepce is a distance from Vitez; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's one-and-a-half hours drive, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This report is a report on the situation of the Zepce 111th Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I've shown you, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, a sample of documents which represent reports back to Colonel Blaskic from the Zenica municipality, the military, 4th Military Police, the Viteska Brigade, the Busovaca Brigade, the Kiseljak Brigade and the Zepce Brigade; and does it appear to you, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, from these exhibits that I've shown you that there was good reporting back to Colonel Blaskic in respect of the combat situation that was occurring in his area of operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the examples you've given me two things spring to mind; firstly, that I think to have an accurate assessment, an accurate assessment of whether reporting was good, you would need to study one order, there is an early one here that went out to about a dozen different units, and confirm that all dozen of them were responding to that order as requested. The other thing that springs to mind, and we are certainly not getting that, there is a general pattern here that we're getting reports from three brigades all the time. The other thing that springs to mind is all these reports, including the one on the -- which was very strange to me -- including the one on the morning of the 16th of April, the report from the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Defence 280.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to that one -- but most of the ones, particularly the first two days of this, they all refer to attacks on their positions by the Muslims. That springs to mind immediately from reading these, which was a trend I was not aware of at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, is this how the British military operates in a combat situation, orders go out and reports come back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but we don't operate in this paper trail system, normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. But, nevertheless, there is a function of command orders going out and reports coming back to the commander; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is. And if I could elaborate slightly. We have reports, there are routine reports which are sent either every 12 or 24 hours, depending on the situation. In the case of Bosnia, we sent 24-hourly reports, as I remember. And then there are combat reports which are sent immediately during the battle so the commander knows what is going on where. And those are two different types of reports. The latter type would normally be sent over the radio immediately. And at battalion level, the other ones would also be sent over the radio. This written type of report is, I think, it's not something I'm very familiar with in the British army, because I think is more concerned with much higher level command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, now I would like to show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/32. Mr. Dundas-Whatley, this is a report authored by Colonel Blaskic, it is a Defence military secret, it is strictly confidential, it is dated the 7th of May 1993 at 1230 hours, and it is addressed to the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, the head of the Defence department of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, and the chief of the main headquarters of the HVO, Mostar, and it is a report on the special situation in Central Bosnia Operation Zone and the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, if I can, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, to the third to the last page, and you will see in Colonel Blaskic's own words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page number?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't have a page number, but if you look at the top there is a series of numbers, and it should be 00564015, do you have that page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the mid-page conclusion? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read, in Colonel Blaskic's own words, his assessment in a confidential military secret to his superior officers about the level of command and control in Central Bosnia. I quote paragraph. "1. Command and control function properly, and all missions proceed in a planned fashion, according to orders, with detailed knowledge of the situation, full coordination and control." Have you ever seen this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is Colonel Blaskic's assessment of how command and control --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that a question, Mr. President, or is counsel lecturing or posturing, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. We don't have a great deal of time. What document are you talking about? I'm having difficulty following you, 456/32?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Since it isn't paginated, what -- it starts with "composition". So, this, the last word is -- the one I have says "demand" at the end. There is some page number, 00621.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, this is the assessment of Colonel Blaskic to his superior officers of how command and control functioned in the Operation Zone, and this assessment of Colonel Blaskic differs from your assessment; does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who do you think had more reliable and more complete information, you, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, or Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have detailed knowledge of the workings of the HVO headquarters so I can only assume Colonel Blaskic's knowledge of his command control system would be better than mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, does it seem probable or possible to you that in a top secret military document sent to the Supreme Commander of the armed forces, who happened to be Mate Boban, the head of the defence department of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, who happened to be Bozo Rajic, and the chief of the main headquarters of the HVO Defence counsel in Mostar, who was General Petkovic, that Colonel Blaskic would be deceiving his superior officers about the level and the degree of command and control that he had over his forces in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you asking me is he likely to deceive them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, lastly, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How much more time do you have? How much more time do you need, Mr. Harmon? I was thinking about the break for the interpreters. We're working until 1.30. What do you have, another ten minutes, about?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you want to take a short break now and then we could start up afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would prefer to continue for the next few minutes, Mr. President, with the line of questioning I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me consult with my colleagues. We will suspend and the hearing and resume in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are going to resume for the last hearing of the week. You have about ten minutes or about 15 minutes. Go ahead. You will finish by 1.00 at the latest and then there is the re-examination -- the time for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, earlier in your examination, when you opined that the command and control of Colonel Blaskic in Central Bosnia was weak, you testified that you had not seen combat orders. I have shown you a number of combat orders that you have testified you have not seen before testifying today, and I have shown you combat orders that were issued by Colonel Blaskic in the Vitez municipalities and the Busovaca municipalities on the 15th and the 16th of April, 1993. I have shown you the Defence Exhibit 267, which is an order -- preparatory combat order dated the 15th of April, 1993 at 10.00, in which Colonel Blaskic says, “In the event of a rather strong attack by Muslim extremist forces from the direction of the villages of Nadioci, Ahmici, Svinjarevo Pirici inform me, and if fire is opened directed on you, return fire and neutralise the attacker." Evidence has been presented in this case that attacks in the Lasva Valley occurred simultaneously in Vitez, Nadioci, Santici, Pirici, Sivirno Selo, Donja Veceriska at 5:30 in the morning on the 16th of April, 1993. I have shown you orders issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 17th of April, 1993, ordering the attack on Gomionica and Svinjarevo at 5.30 in the morning on the following day, and evidence has been presented in this Tribunal that on the following day, at that time, the HVO attacked those villages. I have shown you a number of combat reports sent to Colonel Blaskic by his brigade commanders, and a sample of those reports, incomplete reports, sent to Colonel Blaskic from Zenica municipality, Vitez municipality -- Viteska Brigade I should say, the Busovaca Brigade, the Kiseljak HVO Brigade, the Zepce Brigade and the 4th Military Police, reports that were requested by Colonel Blaskic. Finally, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, you have seen what Colonel Blaskic said to the supreme commander of the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban, what he said to the Defence Minister Bruno Stojic, what he said to his commanding officer General Petkovic on the 7th of May, that, "Command and control function properly and all missions proceed in a planned fashion according to orders, with detailed knowledge of the situation, full coordination and control." Do you still maintain your answer that Blaskic's command and control was poor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but that is a very long -- a very long question, and based on a lot of assumptions. And having had time to think about this in more detail, I would like to just draw your attention to some of the documents which I've been given in the build-up to this very long question to reinforce my opinion. Firstly, if we could deal with the situation with regards to the orders issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 15th of April. He asked that the orders -- that in the case of the 4th Military Police Battalion, that they were expecting an attack, and they should -- if fire is opened, they should return fire and then neutralise the attacker. Then he later says they should send a report. Then the report is here, it's about ten lines long, and the report says that -- and this is the 4th Military Police Battalion referring to the village of Ahmici, that the 4th Military Police Battalion was attacked by the Muslims, and so contrary to the orders that they were given, they went ahead and -- somebody went ahead, and I can only assume it was this unit, because they appear, from these documents, to be based next to Ahmici, went ahead and destroyed that village. So I don't consider the -- although that is not in the report. The report does not say that the village was destroyed. The report does not say that anyone burnt Ahmici or killed a hundred civilians. I think this report by the 4th Military Police Battalion is -- could be described as completely inaccurate and misleading, and if I was Colonel Blaskic sitting in the Hotel Vitez and I received that report, I would believe that things were going very well in that sector of my command. This report is designed to mislead Colonel Blaskic, I believe. It -- also, the events on the ground demonstrate a complete disobeying of his order. His order did not say, "Go and kill 100 civilians." The second issue was the village of Gomionica, which is in the Kiseljak area. It is not a village which I'm familiar with, but according to your -- according to your question earlier, you said that Gomionica was attacked and razed, I believe you said, and all the Muslims were cleansed, or words to that effect, from the village. The report on the village -- and I think we did have the order of what the Kiseljak Brigade was supposed to do in Gomionica, but it certainly was not as you have described they did do. The report does not say that they must cleanse the village, burn it to the ground, which is apparently, according to what counsel has just said, happened, but the report received back on the 18th definitely does not say that's what's happened either. I don't know what day that happened. It may have been after the 18th. But certainly the report after the 18th makes no reference to the ethnic cleansing of that village. Going back to this very large document that you have just quoted, where Colonel Blaskic concludes that the -- to his commander that the command control is functioning properly. If you had taken the time to read the previous page of this document which I have just read, paragraph 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could we, for the record -- I'd just like to note the witness first was referring to Exhibit D280 which is the military report regarding Ahmici, and now he's referring to Prosecutor's Exhibit 56/32, page 014.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's 456/32. About the second paragraph of six he's referring to the Fojnica Battalion. Now, we have an order which you asked me read just now, which was 456/46B, where the Fojnica -- sorry, the Fojnica Battalion is given orders of what it is required to do under its military chain of command. Then in the report that Colonel Blaskic then sends to his commander up the chain, he says, and I quote, “All units to carry out their tasks except the battalion in Fojnica, which with engaged in personnel reshuffling and taking a neutral position vis-à-vis the Muslims. So that the Muslim forces are attacking on Busovaca unimpeded from the area of Fojnica." He is actually telling his commander in Mostar, in a roundabout way, that his orders to the Fojnica Battalion have been ignored, disregarded or disobeyed. So that's the third example from the question which springs to mind, without going through a great deal more. I would also refer you to another paragraph on the same page of this very long report that Colonel Blaskic wrote, and it's at the bottom of that same page, number one. The problem is his communication routes have been cut off, and then he explains how he is now completely cut off from Herzegovina. On the next page, he is completely cut off -- Kiseljak is completely cut off from him, and that Zepce and Usora, which is much further north, are completely cut off from him as well. So I think that in summary, these documents actually do not support your -- the counsel's assertion that command and control was going well, but the reports were misleading, incomplete, and his own report illustrates that to us and to his commander, if his commander wanted to read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified that you disagreed with the a statement, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, “The attack on Ahmici could not have occurred without the authority of Colonel Blaskic, due to the number of troops involved and the scale of the attack," and your answer was, "I disagree. The statement assumes that all of the attacks would have been ordered by Blaskic, and the command and control that existed at the time means that it is probably not the case, almost certainly not the case." Do you maintain your answer in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, do I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you some additional questions, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, and that is about your military career in the British army. You testified, did you not, before this Tribunal that the -- under what circumstances did you leave the army, and your testimony was, “The army went under a large-scale reduction in force and that's when I left." Now, let me explore that with you for just a moment. At the end of the Cold War, the British army decided to reduce its land forces from 155,000 to 100,000 soldiers, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they asked to reduce their soldiers through a programme of what was known as redundancy. There was voluntary redundancy, in other words, soldiers could opt out of the service, get a large capital payment, preserve their retirement benefits and leave the service; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a large number of British officers and soldiers left the British army through a voluntary redundancy procedure, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you testified, and I'm going to quote, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, from your testimony on direct-examination, “In the British army, officers and soldiers, senior NCO, belong to a meritocracy, where they are promoted as a result of being good at their jobs, getting good reports." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the second way the British army reduced its land forces was by compulsory redundancy; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And compulsory redundancy or forced early retirement was a situation where the Ministry of Defence reviewed the personnel file of NCOs and officers in the British military, and desired -- made a decision on the desirability whether those NCOs and officers should remain in the British army, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They retained their best personnel and released their weakest personnel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Arguably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you left the army in 1993 through the programme of compulsory redundancy, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were made redundant in 1993 while you were serving in Bosnia, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the only officer of the Cheshire Regiment serving in Bosnia at the time asked to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make an appeal from this compulsory redundancy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Appeal was made by my commanding officer Bob Stewart, by his commanding officer Brigadier Andrew Cumming, based on the last two years of work in the army both in three tours of Northern Ireland and in my time in Bosnia. Based on my recent two or three years of exceptional, or to use their word, "excellent" reports for those last three years. My commanding officer, my regiment and indeed the brigadier in command of all British forces in Bosnia said the that army was making mistake and so they appealed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the result of that appeal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The appeal was turned down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Ministry of Defence didn't agree with their assessment, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I have been subsequently been asked to go back to Bosnia with the British army. I have been asked on two occasions by the Ministry of Defence to rejoin on a special type commission, and to serve back in Bosnia doing presumably similar work to what I was doing before, and on both occasions I refused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about an interview that you had with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor on July 22, 1998 in Split, Croatia, where you were residing at the time. Mr. Dundas-Whatley, did you have a meeting with Howard Tucker at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Howard Tucker is a British police officer employed with the Office of the Prosecutor, is he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a meeting with Jean-Pierre Kapelle a French retired Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have a meeting also with Patrick Lopez-Terres, a lawyer who is employed by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, did I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they ask you about the events that occurred it Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you inform them that your memory was not very good about the events because you were usually drunk by lunch time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the early part of my tour that is true, although from about the beginning of April, 1993, I almost completely stopped drinking as a liaison officer, which was considered very unusual that liaison officers would not drink, but I stopped drinking because I was going to so many meetings every day that if I continued to drink, I would be an alcoholic. So I stopped probably about the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell them as well, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, when they asked you questions about matters about which you've testified, that "I was quite drunk most of the time." Therefore, you couldn't remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I probably did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I think I if you asked any liaison officer and my commanding officer about dealing with the locals, they would all say the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, at that same meeting with Mr. Patrick Lopez-Terres, Mr. Howard Tucker and Mr. J.P. Kapelle, did you deceive them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell them that you were not intending to testify for either the Defence or the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We may have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think Mr. Harmon's time has expired. We have been -- limits have been imposed on us, and we voluntarily abided by them. My colleague's redirect examination after a two and a half week of cross-examination was limited to under two and a half hours and we abided by those restrictions. I think counsel for the Prosecution should do the same, and if he declines, then the Court should enforce --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand that this reminder of an equal amount of time for both parties is coming at the right time, but these questions and answers do throw the Judges into an abyss of perplexity. The rather idyllic state of the people working in the army at the time is of interest. I'm very sorry, Mr. Hayman, but I think Mr. Harmon has to continue, and the witness is under oath, and is in good physical shape today, and is, therefore, in a position to answer. Mr. Harmon, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, my question was: Did you deceive the three gentlemen I talked about by informing them that you did not intend to testify for the Defence or the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not talking about this case. All the questions and all the answer were is in relation to another case, which at that stage had not even started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently have a conversation with Mr. Tucker on the 23rd of October, 1998, in which you apologised to Mr. Tucker because you had deceived him because you had already reached an agreement to testify for the Defence prior to the conversation that you had with Mr. Tucker in Split on the 22nd of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I will explain. I'll explain. I can understand why you may think there's some deception here. From the very beginning, when I first got involved with the War Crimes Tribunal, which was in May, 1993 when I escorted Mr. Payam Akhavan, I think, around middle Bosnia, from that moment I realised the gravity of the situation. I realised the appalling atrocities that had gone on and how important it was that this should be dealt with on an international level by a neutral party, the International War Crimes Tribunal, which was subsequently put in place. From then on, over a period of four or five years, I have frequently and on many occasions helped the Prosecutors to piece together a lot about what happened. During the course of that, piecing this together and discussing with the Prosecutors, I started to have doubts about some of the -- some of the ways in which not evidence was being gathered, but the ways in which people were being indicted and the reasons behind it. I'm being totally frank and honest with you, but I think you need a full answer to that question. I was repeatedly approached, repeatedly approached, throughout last year and this year by the Defence team in the name of Colonel Blaskic, and I told them exactly what I told the Prosecutors, and that is that I would have -- I had no intention of making a statement, and no intention of taking part in a trial, but I would provide all my photographs and documents and as much information to all sides. Those meetings with the Prosecutors continued, and with the Defence team continued until the beginning of this year, probably about May or June, when I then decided that I was going to, in light of what I remembered and what I knew existed in my notebook, although I still, at that stage, had not recovered all these notebooks, and this has happened in the last three months, two months, that I would -- that I would probably -- I told the Defence team that I would probably be happy to speak in the Defence of Colonel Blaskic because what I remembered about command and control and some of the other major issues. I then was approached again by the Office of the Prosecutors who wanted to talk to me about Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez, and, of course, there was a major overlap between all these Croat people in middle Bosnia. They asked me again to testify. I said I would not. They then asked me would I testify -- if I was approached by the Defence, would I testify for the Defence, and I said, "No." At that stage I was referring entirely to the case they were talking about. I didn't think it was prudent, at that stage, to tell the Office of the Prosecutor that I intended to defend in the case of Colonel Blaskic, and I didn't think it necessary, particularly as the people I was talking to were investigating Cerkez and Kordic. Subsequently, I then went to England, I found all my notebooks which are all here, and my maps, and I brought them here. I have also, yesterday, and frequently this week and last week, I have been in an ongoing dialogue with the Office of the Prosecutor about submitting notebooks or not for other cases, and submitting my photographs for other cases, and it is my intention, next week, to have a meeting in England with Office of the Prosecutor to hand over about 120 films of photographs that were taken during my tour in the British army in Bosnia. I have never at any stage attempted to interrupt the work of the Tribunal. All I want to do is see that everyone gets a fair trial and I'm assisting both sides in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Howard Tucker, on the 22nd of July, 1998, that Mr. Hayman had insisted strongly in involving you as a witness for the Defence in the Blaskic case but that you had refused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not use the name of anyone. I ask not use any names. I said that I had been approached by a Defence team, I said it was an American. He asked me if it was a name -- I think he probably said was it Hayman and I probably shrugged my shoulders. I was being evasive but for the reasons I've explained to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your desire to assist the Prosecutor's Office, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, did you refuse to give a signed statement to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never asked to be a witness in this case by the prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked to sign a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor tried to pull a trick on me by writing a statement themselves and having me sign it, and I said that I had no intention of signing a statement, "Especially not one that you've written yourself."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Dundas-Whatley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What kind of statement are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was -- Your Honour, I think this was probably about a year ago, maybe more. I can't remember when. I was living in Sarajevo and a statement was roughly written out on a piece of paper. One of Prosecutors visited and I gave him as much help as I could, but I said I wasn't going to sign it, I didn't write it, and it wasn't even typed at this stage. It was basically what he wanted me to say. And I think that if I'm going to have to say anything, then I'm going to have to review all my notebooks, which I have done, and I will attend court if I'm going to take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask one additional question with the court's indulgence, please. Who was that investigator, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. I have met a lot of investigators over the last five years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Riad, have you completed your question? Mr. Hayman, you have your right to examination now, but do it with a -- it will be done with a degree of flexibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I estimate -- because of all the documents the witness has been shown and a need to go over some of those documents, I estimate one hour. I estimate I need one hour, and the witness can return on Monday to complete that and the court's examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then we'll come back on Monday. There is no problem with that, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How times were you interviewed by Prosecutors and investigators from the Office of the Tribunal Prosecutor, can you estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you add all the phone calls and the visits and contacts with the Tribunal, it's certainly in excess of 10. I mean, there's been three this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Roughly how many days did you spend with the Office of the Tribunal Prosecutor, prosecutors and investigators, helping them review events that occurred during your tour of duty? Can you estimate that, how much time you gave them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you measure it in terms of days, it's probably three or four. I don't know. Maybe less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you personally interviewed by any of the Prosecutors in this case, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And could you just point to which of the three gentlemen, if it was one or more than one? The gentleman on the far left? Mr. Kehoe, our friend and colleague?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you, after those ten or more contacts, those four days of interviews, that personal interview by Mr. Kehoe, did they ever ask you to come and testify in this case before this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you have come if they'd asked, in the end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once -- once I'd reviewed all my notebooks. In this case it would probably be quite difficult for me to testify for the Prosecution, but because -- because I don't think they'd want to hear a lot of what I would have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I was never asked. What may be of interest also, is I don't think any of the key officers from my regiment who had dealings with the locals have been asked. None of the liaison officers have attended. The military information officer, the operations officer and the commanding officer, none of them who had dealings with the locals have attended as witnesses for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There were a number of documents put before you, and I'll try and organise that for after the recess, the weekend recess, so that we can do it quickly and efficiently, but while the -- some of these are fresh in your mind and in the court's mind, if Exhibit 490A could be retrieved. You were shown an order from Colonel Blaskic to the HVO brigade in Fojnica, to the battalion in Fojnica, to engage in military activity. You may even still have it before you. I've lost track of the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I believe that's so. Do you have it in front you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Does it order the HVO battalion in Fojnica to engage in military activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: While the registrar is looking for the document, let me draw your attention to Exhibit 490A, which I have placed on the ELMO to your left. Can you turn and see it, or do you see it on the screen? This is a document, English translation of a document which has a number of authoring or signatory parties, including the 3rd Fojnica Battalion Command, Fojnica HVO, Croatian Democratic Community, Franciscan Monastery and some other apparently cultural organisations writing to the Operative Zone command in Vitez and the command of the Kiseljak HVO Brigade. Then it references an order, which I can represent to you was an order -- the 20th of April order referenced was an order dismissing the commander of the battalion. If I'm in error and it was another order to engage in the military activity ordered on the 18th of April, and I'm sorry I can't be absolutely specific, I don't have that exhibit or number in front of me; but it references that order, which I represent to you was an order from Colonel Blaskic. The document states, "The command of the battalion has reached the following decision," in all caps. "Your order of 20 April is being completely rejected, due to the work accomplished so far and the complexity of the current situation in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Fojnica Battalion. The Croatian people of Fojnica support this unanimous decision." What does this document tell you about the chain of command within the HVO, particularly with respect to the battalion in Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't got access to the order this is referring to, but this suggests to me that probably Colonel Blaskic wasn't aware of the complex situation in Fojnica, whatever that complex situation is; but far more importantly, it is a refusal to carry out the order. And what makes it so strange, when compared with military orders I'm used to in the British army, is the number of people who have signed this, this not order, this report or this decision, the number of people who are involved in making a decision that the HVO battalion should not carry out its orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it normal for a military commander to be corresponding with a monastery and with a cultural organisation, if you will, over whether the commander's military orders are going to be followed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely not, not in the British army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What kind of chain of command is that? Is it a chain of command, if you issue an order and the local monastery writes back, we reject your decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It reinforces my opinion that the chain of command was, at best, poor, ill-defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with respect to the Fojnica battalion the chain of command was non-existent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was non-existent -- it existed in the sense that they did at least receive the order. This type of refusal would suggest that things were not going very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibits D267, 268 and 269 could be retrieved, those are three orders of Colonel Blaskic. I don't know if they are still in front of the witness, if the usher could help pull them out of the large stack. While those are being sorted out for you, let me ask some preparatory questions. Counsel, on cross-examination, has reviewed certain events with you in the days prior to the 15th and 16th of April, namely the kidnapping of HVO officers in Novi Travnik, the abduction of a brigade commander, Zivko Totic, that is commander of the HVO Brigade in the town of Zenica, the murder of four in his entourage at the time, and an attempted killing of the commander of the Vitezovi independent unit, Darko Kraljevic. Can you tell us, if within the scope of 72 hours those types of attacks occurred on the commanders of a British unit in the field, in combat situations, or in a hostile situation, in confrontation with a potentially hostile enemy force; what would the effect be on that British unit or units, if those types of actions, abductions, murders had been carried out within a 72-hour period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult to imagine the effect that the kidnapping of a British Brigadier would have on things, and if that was coupled with the attempted murder of another unit commander, the murder of his staff officers and bodyguards, the kidnapping of other commanders, I think the affect on the British army in the zone of operation would be devastating.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How would the British army react, say in Northern Ireland, if those events occurred in 72 hours, if you can answer the question without divulging sensitive information? What would the army do? Would it respond to events of that sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I won't talk at all about Northern Ireland, but hypothetically, of course, -- sorry, in another situation, in another part of the world, if these type of events were happening over a period of two or three days, as was happening to the HVO in Bosnia, yes, we would immediately, I'm sure, start conducting investigations, we would erect road blocks and increase the security situation and issue orders to the units to prepare for further attacks of that nature, I should imagine. But I must add, I was a captain in the British army and not a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would, in your view, forces be placed on a higher state of readiness or alert and to be on guard against possible further attacks or abductions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm almost certain that's exactly what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, you have seen, and you hopefully by now have before you exhibits D267, 268 and 269; do you have those orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't got 267, yet, I don't think, unless it is in here somewhere. I will go through it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you could check and tell me which ones you have. We have about five more minutes today in today's session. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have got 269 and 268.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We need 267B, the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, let's start with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have it? This is the order from 15th of April, 10.00 in the morning with a lead-in descriptive paragraph, paragraph 1. And on the second page, assignment is given to the military police battalion, paragraph 2.1, with respect to, and I don't know if this is on the ELMO so others can read it, if there is a copy that would be helpful, if not, I will put my copy on. This portion of paragraph 2.1 includes the direction, "In the event of a rather strong attack by the Muslim extremist forces," et cetera, "inform me, and if the fire is opened directly at you, return the fire and neutralise the attacker." Is that an order for defensive action or offensive action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is, it is a defence style order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And what about the next paragraph, paragraph 2.2, I direct your attention to the last sentence: "The essential assignment is carry out the blockade of the above-sighted forces and to prevent the same from attacking the high command," that is the headquarters; is that an offensive assignment or a defensive assignment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's even, that's more obviously a better word, defence assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In your opinion, this response, as exhibited in Exhibit D267, to the events of the prior 72 hours, is it a measured and proportionate response, or was it a disproportionate response to the threats ongoing against the HVO and the HVO command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think to answer that question I would have to try and put myself in Colonel Blaskic's position at the time, because this is five-and-a-half years ago, and of course, everyone in this room knows a lot more about what really happened. But bearing in mind the information he had available to him and the recent events, probably his headquarters was verging on a state of paranoia and possibly even panic, I think this could be described as a measured response, when put into that perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree, then, that in Exhibit 268B, paragraph 2.1, when Colonel Blaskic ordered units to increase combat readiness, that was also a measured and not a disproportionate response to the events of the prior 72 hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I haven't read the rest of the document, but yes, that paragraph -- yes, it is a logical and responsible thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You, yourself, I'm directing your attention now to Exhibit D269B, you, yourself, as a result of your tour of duty, became familiar with the presence of BH army forces and units in the locations of Kruscica and Vranjska; is that correct? Kruscica being --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know where Kruscica is and I know where Vranjska is, I just want to refresh myself on the map. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree, as set forth in paragraph 2 of that exhibit, an assignment to block those villages and to prevent ingress and egress or entrances to and exits from those villages, and to respond to any attack with precise fire; would that also, in your view, be a measured and not a disproportionate response to the threat that existed as manifested by the events of the prior 72 hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is a measured response. I think this is, from reading this, I get the impression that Colonel Blaskic was very worried that his headquarters was about to be attacked as a result of the paranoia, or whatever I was describing earlier. So, I think it is probably a measured response, in light of how he probably felt at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, if you've finished with the review of those three documents, we will suspend the hearing, and we will resume at 2.00 on Monday, and ask the witness to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 1.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 2nd day of November, 1998 at 2.00 p.m. 24 25
